last_transition_reason: The proof establishes the cyclotomic exponent formula by counting, via the standard factorization q^N - 1 = product_{r|N} Phi_r(q), and converts those counts to the stated floor expressions. It then proves the polynomiality criterion in both directions: nonnegative exponents give a finite product in Z[q], while any negative exponent yields a nontrivial denominator factor that cannot cancel because distinct cyclotomic polynomials are pairwise coprime. The argument matches the lemma sketch and supports the stated role in the assembly.
latest_nl_proof:
Let e_t denote the exponent of Phi_t(q) in the cyclotomic factorization of F_{b,m,d}(q). Since
F_{b,m,d}(q) = product_{i=1}^m (q^(b+d+i) - 1)/(q^(b+i) - 1)
(the minus signs from 1 - q^N cancel), and since for every integer N >= 1 one has q^N - 1 = product_{r|N} Phi_r(q), the exponent of Phi_t(q) in q^N - 1 is 1 exactly when t divides N, and 0 otherwise. By additivity of exponents in products and quotients,
e_t = #{1 <= i <= m : t divides (b+d+i)} - #{1 <= i <= m : t divides (b+i)}.
Equivalently, e_t is the number of multiples of t in {b+d+1, ..., b+d+m} minus the number of multiples of t in {b+1, ..., b+m}.

Now fix any nonnegative integer A and any positive integer t. The number of multiples of t in {A+1, ..., A+m} is floor((A+m)/t) - floor(A/t), because floor(X/t) counts the multiples of t in {1, ..., X}. Applying this with A = b+d and A = b gives

e_t = (floor((b+d+m)/t) - floor((b+d)/t)) - (floor((b+m)/t) - floor(b/t)).

This is exactly the claimed formula for the exponent of Phi_t(q). It also covers m = 0, because then both sets are empty and both floor differences are 0.

Only finitely many e_t are nonzero: if t > b+d+m, then t divides none of the integers appearing in the numerator or denominator factors. Hence
F_{b,m,d}(q) = product_{t >= 1} Phi_t(q)^{e_t}
is really a finite factorization.

We now prove the polynomiality criterion. If e_t >= 0 for every positive integer t, then F_{b,m,d}(q) is a finite product of cyclotomic polynomials, so F_{b,m,d}(q) lies in Z[q] because each Phi_t(q) does. In particular, F_{b,m,d}(q) is a polynomial.

Conversely, suppose some e_r < 0. Write
P(q) = product_{e_t > 0} Phi_t(q)^{e_t},
Q(q) = product_{e_t < 0} Phi_t(q)^{-e_t},
so that F_{b,m,d}(q) = P(q)/Q(q). Then Q(q) is nonconstant, because e_r < 0 and Phi_r(q) is nonconstant. Distinct cyclotomic polynomials have disjoint sets of roots, hence are pairwise coprime in Q[q]. Since e_r < 0, the factor Phi_r(q) occurs in Q(q) but not in P(q); all factors of P(q) are Phi_t(q) with t != r, so Phi_r(q) is coprime to each of them and therefore cannot divide P(q). But if F_{b,m,d}(q) were a polynomial R(q), then P(q) = R(q)Q(q), so every factor of Q(q), in particular Phi_r(q), would divide P(q), a contradiction. Therefore F_{b,m,d}(q) is not a polynomial whenever some e_t < 0.

So F_{b,m,d}(q) is a polynomial if and only if e_t >= 0 for every positive integer t. Using the formula already proved for e_t, this is equivalent to
floor((b+m)/t) - floor(b/t) <= floor((b+d+m)/t) - floor((b+d)/t)
for every positive integer t. In that case, as shown above, F_{b,m,d}(q) actually belongs to Z[q].
role_in_parent: Translates the polynomiality hypothesis into an explicit arithmetic condition on counts of multiples in two equal-length intervals.
statement_nl: For integers b, m, and d with b >= 0, m >= 0, and d >= 0, define F_{b,m,d}(q) := product_{i=1}^m (1 - q^(b+d+i)) / (1 - q^(b+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 when m = 0. For each positive integer t, let Phi_t(q) denote the t-th cyclotomic polynomial. Then the exponent of Phi_t(q) in the cyclotomic factorization of the rational function F_{b,m,d}(q) is (floor((b+d+m)/t) - floor((b+d)/t)) - (floor((b+m)/t) - floor(b/t)). Consequently, F_{b,m,d}(q) is a polynomial in q if and only if floor((b+m)/t) - floor(b/t) <= floor((b+d+m)/t) - floor((b+d)/t) for every positive integer t; in that case F_{b,m,d}(q) actually lies in Z[q].

domain_restrictions: b, m, and d are integers and each is at least 0
t ranges over positive integers only
q is a formal indeterminate, not a numerical parameter
the product defining F_{b,m,d}(q) is finite and uses the convention that the empty product equals 1 when m equals 0
Phi_t(q) is the standard t-th cyclotomic polynomial
the cyclotomic factorization is understood for the rational function in q, so exponents may be interpreted as multiplicities in a factorization of a rational function
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every nonnegative integer triple b, m, d, the t-th cyclotomic polynomial appears in the factorization of F_{b,m,d}(q) with exponent equal to floor((b+d+m)/t) minus floor((b+d)/t) minus floor((b+m)/t) plus floor(b/t), for every positive integer t. Moreover, F_{b,m,d}(q) is a polynomial in q exactly when, for every positive integer t, floor((b+m)/t) minus floor(b/t) is less than or equal to floor((b+d+m)/t) minus floor((b+d)/t); in that case the polynomial has integer coefficients.
quantifier_order: for all integers b, m, d with b, m, d nonnegative
define F_{b,m,d}(q) using the finite product, with the empty product equal to 1 when m equals 0
for each positive integer t, define Phi_t(q) as the t-th cyclotomic polynomial
for each positive integer t, the exponent of Phi_t(q) in the cyclotomic factorization of F_{b,m,d}(q) is the stated floor-expression
for each fixed b, m, d, F_{b,m,d}(q) is a polynomial in q if and only if the stated inequality holds for every positive integer t
in the polynomial case, F_{b,m,d}(q) lies in Z[q]
